subject: Model SEs compared to bootstrapped SEs too large - stacked years approach

messages.author: 76adbf22c1d1c19e
messages.subject: Model SEs compared to bootstrapped SEs too large - stacked years approach
parts:
Hi everyone, 

My question concerns the bootstrapping that is done after using the stacked years approach (where site/years = sites). There was an earlier thread about this approach (https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/OHkk98y09Zo). 

When I took this approach and looked at the ratio of the standard error from the model (SE) to the standard error from the bootstrap (SE.bs) - and the same for the confidence interval length (cil/cil.bs) - , my ratios for this for some parameters were >100 (a couple were in the 200s). 

I am using the code provided in the chapter proof from the AHM book as a guide (thanks to Andy Royle for this!), and in that example code, none of the ratios were >100. 

Does anyone have any idea what might be going on, or if this is OK? It seems to mean that my SEs and CILs from my original model are much larger than from the bootstrap (at least for some parameters). It seems like this is the opposite of what should happen, since the idea with stacked data is that it might understate the uncertainty, hence the reason for the bootstrap. 

Background: I'm using a compilation of different citizen science datasets over a very large area (~90k km2) which I've split into 1 km2 grid cells as different "sites". It's a bit of a trick to get the data to comply with occupancy modeling assumptions because of how it was collected - and that reduced the data available. Could the small amount of data in relation to the large area be what is causing the problem? Or perhaps I'm just missing something more obvious? 

Thank you so much for your help!!
Autumn

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Model SEs compared to bootstrapped SEs too large - stacked years approach
parts:
I think that without the actual data and code one wouldn't be able to pin down the issue.

However, using the site as the bootstrap unit of replication keeps the likely positive correlation among years at a site resulting in smaller standard errors.  (Yes, that's stated a bit loosely).  Now here's an analogy that's maybe even looser:  Suppose you have paired data that would typically be used in a paired t-test.  But for some reason you want to ignore the pairing and perform a two-sample t-test.  But to your rescue is the bootstrap selecting the pair as the bootstrap unit of replication.  Doing so gets you back to the smaller standard errors associated with the paired t-test.

Jim
